passage:
Dear Tanuja,

You asked how the freelance job is going, so here is the honest version. The client sent back my brochure design with three lines: "Make the blue bigger. Change the font. Fine otherwise." No questions, no mention of the brief I spent a week on. I sat there feeling as if the work was invisible, and I even wondered if I am simply not good at this.

Then I remembered what you told me last spring about pinning things down. So I wrote back: "Who should the blue speak to? Can you confirm the final font and the sign-off date?" The client replied within an hour, with real answers. Nothing about my work had changed, only my questions. I will keep asking. Thank you for the nudge.

Love,
Nikita

qa.q: What did the client's message say about the brochure design?
qa.a: The client wrote "Make the blue bigger. Change the font. Fine otherwise." with no questions.

qa.q: How did Nikita feel when the reply came, and what shows it?
qa.a: Nikita felt the work was invisible and even wondered about being "simply not good at this", which shows how much the short reply stung.

qa.q: What could Nikita do next time a client replies with so little?
qa.a: Ask direct questions, such as who the design should speak to and what the final font and sign-off date are, so decisions get pinned down.

qa.q: How might Tanuja read this letter?
qa.a: Tanuja may be glad that the earlier advice about pinning things down worked, and may notice that the client's silence was never a verdict on Nikita's quality.

grounding: A client barely engages with the work and Nikita moves from demoralised to asking direct questions instead of internalising the disinterest.
